Which Grouper Did I Catch? Tampa Bay & Gulf Grouper ID

Pulled a grouper off the bottom and aren't sure which one it is? Start with the markings and fins. Here's what to look for around Tampa Bay and out in the Gulf.

By Catch 'N Bake · 6 minute read
Published September 14, 2026 · Updated September 14, 2026
Sources checked September 14, 2026. Check linked agencies for changes before fishing.

In this articleStart with the fish in front of youWhich grouper belong in the Tampa Bay bridge conversation?Gag grouper: look for the winding marksGoliath grouper: small ones count, tooRed grouper: pale patches on a reddish fishBlack grouper: check the blocks and fin edgesScamp: take a look at the tailYellowmouth, yellowfin, and other Gulf groupersGet a useful photo without holding up the releaseCan I keep the grouper I caught?

Start with the fish in front of you

A grouper caught around a Tampa Bay bridge and one caught on a Gulf reef can send you to different parts of the identification guide. Take a look at the whole fish before deciding. Body markings, fin shape, and the cheek can help you sort it out.

This guide starts with gag, goliath, red, black, and scamp. It also covers yellowmouth and yellowfin lookalikes, plus other names you may see on a Gulf grouper list. They don't all use the same water, and a catch location alone won't settle the identification.

  • Gag: winding dark marks along the side.
  • Goliath: a heavy body, rounded tail, and small dark spots on the head and fins.
  • Red grouper: reddish brown with pale blotches.
  • Black grouper: more rectangular blotches and brassy spots.
  • Scamp: clusters of small spots, with extended tail rays in adults.

Use those clues to choose a closer comparison below. Check more than one feature before calling it.

Which grouper belong in the Tampa Bay bridge conversation?

Gag and goliath are worth learning before fishing bay structure. FWC places young gag in estuaries and seagrass beds. Young goliath also use estuaries, including bridges, docks, and other structure. Those habitat descriptions give you a sensible place to start your comparison when a small grouper comes up near the pilings. FWC gag profile and FWC goliath profile.

Florida State Parks lists grouper among the catches at the Skyway fishing piers, but that doesn't identify the fish on your line. Before heading there, check the park access notices and fishing requirements. The park has posted access restrictions and an annual education requirement. Follow the current signs rather than an old video showing somebody fishing farther down the pier.

If you're fishing from a boat, leave room around other anglers and keep navigation channels clear. Have a release plan before dropping beside a high bridge or seawall.

Gag grouper: look for the winding marks

Gag often have a gray or brown body with dark marks that wind across the sides. Check the pale edging on the anal fin and tail, too. The lower cheek plate, called the preopercle, has a pronounced serrated spur. Look at it without putting your fingers near the gills or sharp edges.

Black grouper are a frequent identification mixup. Compare the pattern and cheek together instead of deciding from how dark the fish looks. Compare your fish with FWC’s gag reference.

Our St. Pete gag season article covers trip planning. The gag cooking guide covers a legal keeper once you're home.

Goliath grouper: small ones count, too

A goliath doesn't have to be huge. Look for a thick body, small eyes, a rounded tail, and little dark spots on the head and fins. Dark bars may show along the side. FWC describes young fish using mangroves and built structure in estuaries, which is why size alone is a poor way to rule one out. FWC goliath identification.

Keep a goliath release simple.

FWC requires immediate release unless you hold the required harvest permit and tag and meet the program's rules. Do not lift a large goliath onto a boat or pier. FWC recommends keeping smaller ones in the water, too. A photo must not delay release. Read the goliath handling and permit rules.

The limited permit fishery has its own season and areas. It isn't part of an ordinary gag grouper trip.

Red grouper: pale patches on a reddish fish

Look for a reddish brown body with uneven white blotches, small black dots on the snout, and an orange to scarlet lining inside the mouth. FWC also notes a long second dorsal spine. Red grouper use bottom habitat, including nearshore reefs and offshore hard bottom. FWC red grouper reference.

Use the mouth color only when you can already see it. There's no need to extend handling to force a better look. Compare the body pattern with the other features you have.

If you've confirmed a legal red grouper, our red grouper taste and cooking guide has preparation ideas.

Black grouper: check the blocks and fin edges

Black grouper have dark, roughly rectangular blotches with brassy spots on an olive or gray body. The outer portions of the soft dorsal, anal, and tail fins are dark. The bottom of the cheek plate is more rounded than the serrated spur on a gag. FWC black grouper reference.

FWC associates adults with rocky bottoms, reefs, and dropoffs, while juveniles can occur inshore. Include black grouper in your Gulf comparisons, but don't call a dark fish a black grouper without checking its pattern.

Scamp: take a look at the tail

Scamp have small dark or reddish spots that can group into rosette patterns on a pale gray or brown body. Adults develop extended rays at the top and bottom of the tail. Think of a few longer strands along those edges when you're comparing a clear photo.

FWC lists reefs, ledges, and rocky bottom as scamp habitat. This is another fish to learn for trips out of St. Pete into the Gulf. A small scamp may not show the adult tail clearly. FWC scamp reference.

Yellowmouth, yellowfin, and other Gulf groupers

Yellowmouth grouper can resemble scamp. Look for a tan or brown body with small dark spots and yellow inside the mouth and at its corners. FWC describes yellowmouth as less common than scamp in the Gulf and limits its listed range to southern Florida. It's a useful comparison for a wider Gulf trip, rather than a fish to assume you'll find under a Tampa Bay bridge. FWC yellowmouth reference.

Yellowfin grouper can resemble black grouper. Look for oval groups of dark spots arranged in rows and bright yellow across the outer third of the pectoral fins, the paired fins just behind the gills. FWC describes reef habitat from coastal to offshore waters. FWC yellowfin reference.

FWC's Gulf regulations also list rock hind, red hind, coney, graysby, yellowedge, misty, Warsaw, speckled hind, and snowy grouper. That broader list isn't a list of common Tampa Bay bridge catches. If your fish doesn't fit the comparisons here, use the official reef fish identification guide and the species references in the Gulf grouper rules. Don't force an unfamiliar fish into the closest familiar name.

Get a useful photo without holding up the release

Keep the head, body, and tail in the frame. Avoid covering the side with a hand, and keep the original photo so you can crop a copy later. Filters and heavy shadows can make the markings harder to compare.

Have the camera ready before handling a fish. Wet your hands, support it, and keep handling brief. Follow the separate goliath guidance above for those fish. FWC fish handling guidance.

A suggested identification in an app can help you start the comparison. It doesn't establish that the fish is legal to keep. If you can't confirm the species and retention rules, release it promptly.

Can I keep the grouper I caught?

Check the species, your fishing location, the current season, size limits, and bag limits together. Gulf and Atlantic rules differ, and some requirements depend on state or federal waters. Nassau grouper harvest is prohibited, and goliath has the separate permit program described above. Check the current FWC grouper regulations.

Once you've confirmed a keeper, keep it cold and follow the landing requirements. Save the species and a few trip notes while you still remember the details.

Remember what worked.

Use a clear photo in Catch 'N Bake for a suggested fish identification, then compare it with the fish and the official references. Save the confirmed species with your catch notes. Check harvest rules separately before keeping it. Get Catch 'N Bake on the App Store.
